title: Bikes & Trikes
strapline: Pedalling, steering and delivering important parcels — strong legs and quick decisions on every lap.
intent: Build leg strength, stamina and coordination through pushing, scooting and pedalling.
Develop steering, braking and spatial judgement — reading the space and the riders around you.
Learn to wait, take turns and share a limited number of much-wanted wheels.
Grow imaginative journey play — bus routes, deliveries, breakdowns, the car wash.
Understand simple road-sense ideas: stop, go, one way, looking before you pull out.
Feel the deep satisfaction of a physical skill won through practice — from scooting to proper pedalling.
implementation: Set a clear circuit with chalk lines, arrows and a roundabout so riders flow rather than collide.
Use a sand timer at the 'bike park' for turns — children hand over the timer, not the adult.
Commentate on movement: 'You leaned into that corner', 'Your pushing feet have turned into pedalling feet.'
Join the story rather than directing it — be the customer waiting for a pizza, the mechanic, the traffic jam.
Add real jobs: a petrol pump (lengths of hose), a car wash (sponges and spray bottles), number plates to match to parking bays.
Scaffold the almost-pedallers: balance bikes first, then a steadying hand on the back, then let go quietly.
Step back once flow is established — riders negotiating their own near-misses is where the learning is.
key_questions: Where is your bike going today — and what will you do when you get there?
How can we make sure everyone who's waiting gets a turn?
What do your legs have to do differently to get up the slope?
What could we use to build a petrol station on the circuit?
How will the other riders know which way you're going?
What happened when the two trikes met at the corner — what could you try next time?

impact.text: Children progress from scooting along on balance bikes to pedalling trikes with real control, steering round corners and stopping where they mean to.
Younger riders push, pull and heave with purpose — towing trailers, loading crates onto the back, pushing a friend up the slope.
Riders judge speed and space, weaving through the chalk circuit and around walkers without collisions.
Children wait at the bike park with the sand timer, hand over a trike when their turn ends, and increasingly sort the queue out with words before an adult arrives.
Journey play is narrated aloud — 'I'm the delivery man, this parcel's for the baby room' — with roles, routes and breakdowns woven in.
Riders use position and comparison talk naturally: behind, next to, round the roundabout, faster, the long way.
By the time they leave us for school, children ride, brake and dismount with confidence and control, and move because it feels good.

enhancements: Chalk road markings, zebra crossing and a lollipop sign — one child directs the traffic.
A petrol station corner: lengths of hose, a keypad from an old calculator, laminated price signs.
Car wash day: buckets of soapy water, sponges and a 'drying towel' finish line.
Number plates on each trike matched to numbered parking bays for a self-checking park-up at tidy time.
A delivery office: parcels wrapped in brown paper, a trolley, addresses that riders 'read' and deliver around the garden.
A simple ramp or slope section — how do your legs feel going up compared with coming down?
Puncture repair garage: real (blunt) tools, a pump, and a mechanic's checklist to tick off.

playing_exploring: Children choose their vehicle, their route and their story — the circuit is theirs to invent on.
New challenges (the slope, the roundabout, the trailer) are tried out with relish.
active_learning: Almost-pedallers keep trying — feet slipping off, finding the pedals again — until the wheels finally turn.
Riders adjust after a near-miss or a toppled trailer rather than giving up on the game.
creating_thinking: Children turn the same circuit into a bus route, a racetrack or a delivery round, changing the rules as they go.
They find their own solutions: a queue for the pump, a shortcut, a tow rope for a broken-down friend.
